title: Insanely Twisted Shadow Planet
text: Well, this game certainly hit me out of nowhere.  I had grabbed Insanely Twisted Shadow Planet as the next title to play through on my ever-expanding list of “Games I Must Play,” and was very pleasantly surprised. The controls are tight, the visuals are very striking, and the sound design is very fitting. Overall, this is a very complete package, good for a few hours of fun.  I’ve found that I greatly enjoy “Metroidvania” titles, and this game fits that descriptor perfectly. You progress linearly from point A to point B, collect a new power-up and defeat a boss, then use said power-up to continue on to the next area that was previously blocked. The game map is relatively small, and the game can be powered through in roughly four or five hours, but forward progression happens at a steady rate and you never feel slowed or frustrated with any given puzzle.  There really isn’t much of a storyline – there’s no voice acting, and any story is relayed through orchestrated cutscenes that give you the bare-bones minimum that you need to know: you’re an alien, and your planet has been attacked by some type of strange mechano-orgranic virus that corrupts the environment’s flora and fauna against you. Your little alien character decides to do something about this, and from that point, you’re off and running.  I had only expected to play this game for one quick playthrough, but the more I completed the story the more that I saw that I would be coming back to this title again in the future. Secret areas hide in plain sight and wait patiently for you to uncover the correct ability to retrieve them.  The only gripe that I may have with this game is the fact that it is somewhat hard to backtrack to previously explored areas once you have traveled through them. This became an issue once I had defeated a boss, then accidentally progressed forward without picking up the power-up that they had left behind. Thankfully, it wound up not making a difference to the storyline for future puzzles, but it felt strange completing the game and having a gap in my ability wheel.  At any rate, this game is recommended to anyone – the price point during sales is very cheap, and the show you get for the price of admission is a steal. Any fan of “Metroidvania” titles deserve to pick this game up without hesitation, as it’s a title that you’ll probably find yourself going back to a few more times just for kicks.

title: Insanely Twisted Shadow Planet
text: Insanely Twisted Shadow Planet is a 2D side-scrolling action/adventure Metroidvania game with puzzle elements. Basically you fly around in a small flying saucer and solve small puzzles while fighting off enemies and gigantic bosses. As you travel through the shadow planet you will get new abilities that allow you to backtrack to previous areas to open new areas like any Metroidvania type game, though most of the collectibles you find by backtracking are concept art pieces and short movie clips. The art style and music create a very nice atmosphere, and the controls are fairly smooth. Most of the special abilities you get are very creative and fun to use, my favorite being the buzzsaw. There's not a lot of tutorials or hints, but there's an objective marker and you get an info tool you can point at things to find out how to interact with them. All-in-all it was a very good game in my opinion and it's only about 8 hours to play through the entire game and find all of the collectibles. I recommend picking it up sometime.

title: Insanely Twisted Shadow Planet
text: This is a neutral recommendation. The gameplay is solid, metroidvania-style spaceship shoot'em up. The puzzles and fighting can get rather difficult at times, but never unfair. If you fail a few times you will recognise patterns and you'll eventually get it. You end up getting about 10 different weapons to play with, but the ones you get near th end of the game end up being just utility/physics in a very few niche situations. It just seems to work that way with these type of shooters, and it doesn't really change gameplay dramatically enough for any refreshing changes. One thing I like to see in metroidvania games are mobility abilities and this game lacks them. The game tries convey a story through very short cutscenes and gameplay and while it works at getting the story through, it didn't work well at making a compelling narrative. I would have preferred some dialog but I can see why they choose this style. It just didn't jive with me. Same goes for the art style. It works well for the game and is unique without being 16-bit pixel indie game graphics, but I would have preferred more colors than black in every scene, even though you are on a "shadow planet". Just personal preference, I guess.

title: Insanely Twisted Shadow Planet
text: ITSP is a decent game that falls short of being good. You spend the game flying around in a ship killing easy enemies, solving simple puzzles, getting new weapons and powerups, and occasionally fighting easy bosses.  Not much more too it than that.  There's no real plot, stories, dialogue, or characters in the game, which is fine for what it is.  The game is pretty short despite it having a tutorial area and 5 main environments that you'll go through.  Dying is handled  with a quick respawn at the closest checkpoint, which are located all over the place. So on the positive side, the game does look and sound nice.  Controls are solid for the most part with a controller.  Plenty of enemy types. On the downside, the game is very easy.  Most enemies go down quickly and you'll probably spend a lot of the time just driving by them since they pose so little of a threat.  Checkpoints are all over the place and refill your health, so getting damaged often is no problem.  You would expect the difficulty to ramp up as you go along, but surprisingly the final environment is probably both the shortest and easiest to get through. Bosses will barely put up a struggle before you kill them, even the final boss.  Almost all of them allow you to farm health during the battle.  You'll die on occasion but it'll usually be due to something unexpected insta killing you or simply because you were rushing and didn't care enough to slow down.  Puzzles are very simple and barely require any thought.  There are 8 switchable weapons throughout the game but a couple of them are used in 1 environment and then you'll never use them again.  Occasionally the camera can be annoying.  It auto-zooms in and out depending on where you're at.  There are times when it zooms in too closely when you'd prefer that it be further out.  It also has some trouble at keeping up with your ship if you're moving too fast, this is especially noticeable in the wind tunnel areas. Annoyances -  1. Some players have had game slowdown problems.  On my playthrough, there were certain spots where the game would run at about half the normal speed.  Not a huge issue since it goes away once you get away form those spots, but quite noticeable.  2.  The grabber weapon can be frustrating at times, sometimes not grabbing the things you tell it to grab.  3.  There can be an occasional glitch.  One zone has you reflecting light beams off of movable ice shards.  Sometimes they don't reflect properly and require you to fuss around with them until the game decides it wants to act properly.  4.  Whoever designed the campaign menu deserves to be punched in the face.  When you use a controller and select to play the campaign, it brings up 2 options; New Game and Resume Game.  The menu designer didn't bother putting any noticeable icon next to the one you're actually highlighting, so the only way you can tell which one you're selecting is that one is highlighted white while the other is highlighted purple.  Differentiating by color is completely useless when there are only two options and you can't tell which color is the actual highlight color.  Accidentally started a new game when I meant to resume my game.  You can only have one save file, and when you start a new game it automatically saves over your old one.  So I had the fun of beating the tutorial area and the first 2 environments over again.  Was it really too much work to put a damn arrow or something there to show which one you're selecting? ITSP isn't a bad game, but the ease of the game means it lacks any sort of challenge or excitement.  The game doesn't have anything else to fall back on since there's no plot, characters, or dialogue.  The final environment is really a letdown when you get through it and barely have to apply any effort while doing so.  Game simply needs to be more difficult, especially the majority of the boss battles.

title: Interstellar Rift
text: HEAD'S UP: I cannot speak to the game's actual core gameplay, as I haven't tried it, nor do I really intend to as odd as it sounds. I am STRICTLY REVIEWING THE SHIP EDITOR here. If that's what you wanna read about, please, carry forward. I'm an interesting case. I bought Interstellar Rift specifically for ship design. I'm an engineer at heart and I love building things. Spaceships? Pretty high up on the list of "awesome things to create" I think. I've tried many games to get my fix. Kerbal Space Program scratched the rocketry itch, but didn't offer me the nitty-gritty of internals. Building rooms, placing systems, connecting a power grid... I tried Space Engineers, but I'm a rather impatient man. As good as Space Engineers is, the building aspect didn't give me the freedom I wanted, as even in Creative you have to do everything in first person and it gets a bit fiddly. Starship Corporation has a ton of promise, but confines me to set fuselages. It'll be great fun as a corporate management game going forward, but it's not what I'm after in terms of absolute design freedom. Kinetic Void is okay as far as externals, but the internals are a matter of "click on a section, select systems that are in there somewhere" which isn't the complexity I'm after. (Plus it kind of... stopped updating.) So as I'm starting up my first tabletop campaign of Uncharted Worlds with a friend (highly recommend it if you're a tabletop roleplayer by chance), I decided I wanted to give this search another go, and I noticed this $15 Early Access game I'd kept putting off trying. It was time. Enter Interstellar Rift. It. Is. MAGNIFICENT. It takes the basic premise of constructing ships in Space Engineers and simplifies the mechanics to drag-and-click, with tons of systems placed in a matter not unlike placing furniture in The Sims. It requires that life support, power, all that good stuff be accounted for. While it's maybe not perfectly complex (IE, you don't have to manually build ventillation shafts to connect your fans to your life support), it does an excellent job of balancing availability with depth. I can build a little maneuverable heavy fighter akin to Elite: Dangerous' Cobra, a bulky freighter the likes of which I couldn't even access in Elite: Dangerous, all the way up to a huge capital ship the likes of which would make xenos the galaxy over tremble... All by clicking and dragging. And the best part? I can walk around my ship, and should I so desire, even take it out and do stuff with it (then again, that's getting into core gameplay, which again is NOT WHAT I'M REVIEWING, I haven't touched it.) This perfect marriage of simplicity and freedom, having an easy to use placement system while still providing mechanical depth and potentially grand scale... This is EXACTLY what I've been searching for, for the better part of five years. For the ship editor alone, it was worth my $15, no question. DISCLAIMER: If you want more than just a ship editor, please don't assume it'll be worth YOUR $15. Best to look to other reviews first. If your unique tastes match up with mine, however, and a game that lets you build the internals and externals of your ship with minimal fiddling... Don't overlook this. Seriously, don't.

title: Interstellar Rift
text: Currently, this is a very open ended simulator, with the primary focus on building your own ships. You can design anything you want from building a basic shuttle to copying your favorite sci-fi series ship. (Or build a 1:1 scale death star if your really ambitious.) Even if you don't like to build, you can just grab ships from the workshop and fly. Outside the building aspects however, the content is fairly sparce. There are aliens (and other players if your inclined) to fight against, but the quests are fairly generic and the lack of story and NPC characters may drive off some folks. Gaining the resources to build your creations is, thankfully, rather simple. You just fly to an asteroid field and start up your extractors, then refine the ore (sometimes several times). It's no harder then just moving around crates that are given to you. Alternatively, you can earn money in the missions and just buy the resources from a trading station. If you like to design your ships all the way down to utility grids and aestetics, this is a good buy currently. If your not a fan of building and rather dive into an exciting and vibrant game world, your better off waiting.

title: Interstellaria
text: This game was dissapointing at first because I expected something a little more action packed. The game is essentially building empire mixed with a farming game. Your main goal is to collect money to become more powerful via ships or equipment for crew. This lets you progress. Here's the issue, it's not always fun. Ship combat is very fun and high stakes, as one wrong move can mean ten-thousand credits down the drain. Man to man isnt. If you have a better gun and armor, you win. There's not a real battle, especially since you can head back to the ship and heal once you get the medi-station. You just eliminate enemies, by clicking and fast-forwarding until it's done, and then tell everyone to farm the planet. Now that the bad issue is out, lets talk about good. The game has the charm of a nice space game, kinda giving a more exploration based FTL feel (Reccomend that game waaay more though) and keeps you interested. There is actually a story besides "You are captain, explore" and it matches goofy with a slight tinge of sad to make a very good feel. So, in conclusion, buy this game, but don't be ashamed to ask for a refund if the game is not for you.

title: Interstellaria
text: Take my review with a grain of salt but Interstellaria is a game I want to like but every time I boot it up it not only fails to wow me, it generally irks me pretty quickly.  The biggest issue I have with this game is the damn UI.  It has that nineties style of user interface where everything is on screen, you have  a map in the lower right hand corner, and your ship info in the lower left hand corner, and the action takes place up top.  The biggest problem is that when you need to do anything, rather than taking over one of these perfectly good windows, another one pops up.  Need to equip that thing you picked up?  Open two windows, give them some seperation and then go about your business.  Wheeeee!  Second issue is combat, since another pop-up window covers your screen.  The one you need to manage your crew.  So you need to move this window around to be able to access your ship, while also moving your ship via this window and potentially moving your crew via another.  If that sounds fun, flip my thumb around for you but for me it just comes off as badly designed. The other part of this is that I guess the management parts just don't really excite me either.  In FTL you are absolute ruler of your ship, deciding where people need to be to work systems, patch holes and fight off intruders.  In Interstellaria I guess it has that same premise but from the side and with the minor addition of some Sims-like needs?  Your crew also needs to eat and sleep.  I think they take care of these things themselves sometime?  Sometimes you need to land on planets and loot stuff, and I think you fight once in a while (though fighting is basically zerg-swarm each enemy) and then you click the harvest button and wait a while. This is yet another space game I sort of hoped would scratch my particular itch for the genre but really fell flat.

title: Intrusion 2
text: Intrusion 2 is basically an old school side scroller shooting arcade game.  You shoot enemies, pick up weapons, and shoot more enemies.  The game is challenging, like old school arcade games are, making you work fairly hard to get through each level, and there is no health regenerating mechanism so you can easily die if you're not careful but there are checkpoints in each level to respawn at.  The level design is pretty good but nothing that is very exciting, which is what I would consider to be the only minor downside of the game.  What I enjoyed the most are the boss fights.  They can be frustrating to play, but when you beat them it feels incredibly rewarding.  It is a pretty short game, but I would recommend playing this title. As an interesting note, this game was made by just one peson.

title: Intrusion 2
text: INTRUSION 2 is a 2D run n' gun action platformer along the lines of Metal Slug or more vaguely Contra. This is one badass, fun game, with epic, memorable bosses and creative elements like some pretty basic physics and destruction. You can destroy log bridges to send everyone falling to their doom, blow up the supports of watchtowers. Crush enemies under boulders you push over. Physics like that, which add to the fun. The enemies can take a beating and the weapons feel good, but even if there is a variety of weapons, not many feel different from one another. The levels seem like a marathon. They are so long you might find yourself wondering when they end. This is probably good. Earlier I mentioned epic bosses. I don't use that term lightly. It makes me feel weird, but let me tell you about the first boss, a helicopter or hovercraft with arms with multiple phases. If its not shooting at you, its dropping soldiers out. If its not trying to hand pound you into the ground, its literally crawling after you. Its insane and awesome. It is very memorable and covers a lot of ground. To keep things fresh, you can pilot mech suits... if not grab the gun off of a destroyed mech and use it on your enemies. Oh and if that's too normal for you, in the first level, you can ride a giant Arctic wolf. Its pretty nice. The game is challenging, you do have a health bar, and ammo depletes, and you can die more from the controls than you do anything else, BUT the game is very forgiving, with plenty of checkpoints. The controls take a bit of getting use to. You have your standard jump, duck and weapon switch keys, but then to aim you use your mouse. This allows for more precise aim, but I'm more used to the Contra controls of having 8 direction shooting instead of precision. If you're used to Teraria, you'll be used to this. There is floaty jumping that can take some getting used to and the physics seem really light and springy. The boxes will bounce around if lightly nudged. Some of the animation is springy like old cartoon characters. That is probably Flash animation for you. It took a while to get over it, but when I did, I found this game to be really fun to play. There are crazy Holy♥♥♥♥♥♥moments, and moments where the physics can have some unique experiences for a 2D run n gun game, such as seeing a mech jump onto a floating box. The box bounced the mech up and kinda floated away just enough for a giant fish to eat the mech. That wasn't supposed to happen, but it did, and it was cool. Well worth $10.

title: Intrusion 2
text: A sidescrolling shooter against human and mechanized enemies.  The most unique feature is the physically simulated animation used for some of the larger mecha enemies: their individual limbs separately clamber over the crates and barrels that you will try to put between yourself and them. The controls are also great, and the player character is made fast, agile, and capable of dodging. But mainly, the game is well paced and aesthetically pleasing.  New enemies are constantly introduced, and their weapons are spectacular enough that it's fun just to study them.
